name: EaseMate AI
subcategory: multimodal chat plus image and video generation
tagline: One web app that bundles AI chat, text-to-image, and text-to-video behind a single free-to-start account.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The product is a front end over models it does not own: chat, image, video, all rented from upstream providers. An agent can clone the shell in a session, streaming chat with history, an image tab, a video tab, local storage, and it will feel close to the original. What it cannot clone is the economics: you go from a free tier someone else subsidises to paying per generation at list price, and video is the expensive part. The second gap is access, since the headline video models are often gated, waitlisted, or only resold through aggregators, so your build may quietly fall back to whatever you can actually call. Worth building if you already hold API keys and mostly want chat with occasional images; not worth it if the free video quota was the whole appeal.
coreLoopDIY: A local multimodal console with tabbed chat, text-to-image, and text-to-video, each calling a provider API with your own keys and saving every result to a local gallery.
requirements: An OpenAI-compatible API key for chat and images
A Replicate or similar aggregator token for video models
A credit card, since video generation bills per second of output
Local disk for the media gallery
whatYouLose: The free tier, which is the actual draw; your version bills from the first click
Access to whichever frontier video model is currently hyped, if it is gated or resold only through the vendor
Mobile use without hosting your own build somewhere
Prompt presets, aspect ratio and style pickers, and the small usability work that makes generation tools tolerable
Any content moderation or safety layer, which matters more than people expect once you share output
moatNotes: Buying model capacity in bulk and giving it away free is the business. That is a cash position, not a technology moat, and it evaporates when upstream prices move.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because aggregators compress three vendor relationships, three billing accounts, and three sets of rate limits into one tab and one card. For someone who generates a few images a week and wants to try a video model without reading provider docs, that convenience is genuinely worth a subscription. The moment usage gets heavy or specific, the markup over raw API pricing stops making sense and people move to direct keys.
notes: Thin wrappers are the easiest thing in this directory to rebuild and the hardest thing to rebuild cheaply.
prompt:
Build a local multimodal AI console called "Console" in an empty folder.

Stack, no substitutions: Next.js 15 with the App Router, TypeScript, Tailwind, and better-sqlite3 for local persistence. No auth, no cloud database, no telemetry, no analytics. Single user, runs on localhost.

Three tabs in one layout: Chat, Image, Video.

Chat: streaming responses from an OpenAI-compatible chat completions endpoint. Conversations persist in SQLite with a sidebar list, rename, and delete. Model name is configurable in a settings panel and stored in SQLite, not hardcoded.

Image: a prompt box, a size selector, and a count selector. Calls the OpenAI images endpoint. Save returned images to ./media as files, write a row to SQLite with prompt, model, and timestamp.

Video: a prompt box, a duration selector, and an aspect ratio selector. Calls Replicate, creates a prediction, polls until complete, downloads the result to ./media, writes a row. Show an explicit cost warning above the submit button and a confirm step, because video bills per second.

Gallery: a fourth route at /gallery that reads the SQLite media table and shows every generated image and video with its prompt, newest first, with a delete button that removes the row and the file.

Secrets: OPENAI_API_KEY, OPENAI_BASE_URL, REPLICATE_API_TOKEN in .env.local only. Ship .env.example. Never log keys. All provider calls happen in route handlers, never from the browser.

Errors: surface the provider's actual error message in the UI. Do not swallow failures or show a generic toast.

Out of scope: user accounts, billing, sharing links, image editing, upscaling, mobile layout beyond basic responsive Tailwind.

Deliver a README with setup steps, the exact npm commands, and a blunt note that every generation costs real money at provider list prices.
